sum: Shareholders might have noticed that SoftBank Group Corp. (TSE:9984) filed its half-yearly result this time last week. The early response was not positive, with shares down 6.1% to JP¥3,738 in the past week. Revenues beat expectations by 11% to hit JP¥2.2t, although earnings fell badly short, with SoftBank Group reported a statutory loss of JP¥197 per share even though the analysts had been forecasting a profit. The analysts typically update their forecasts at each earnings report, and we can judge from their estimates whether their view of the company has changed or if there are any new concerns to be aware of. We've gathered the most recent statutory forecasts to see whether the analysts have changed their earnings models, following these results.

Taking into account the latest results, the most recent consensus for SoftBank Group from 15 analysts is for revenues of JP¥8.59t in 2027. If met, it would imply a credible 3.6% increase on its revenue over the past 12 months. Statutory earnings per share are expected to crater 72% to JP¥64.41 in the same period. In the lead-up to this report, the analysts had been modelling revenues of JP¥8.54t and earnings per share (EPS) of JP¥132 in 2027. The analysts seem to have become more bearish following the latest results. While there were no changes to revenue forecasts, there was a large cut to EPS estimates.

The consensus price target held steady at JP¥7,667, with the analysts seemingly voting that their lower forecast earnings are not expected to lead to a lower stock price in the foreseeable future. There's another way to think about price targets though, and that's to look at the range of price targets put forward by analysts, because a wide range of estimates could suggest a diverse view on possible outcomes for the business. The most optimistic SoftBank Group analyst has a price target of JP¥11,100 per share, while the most pessimistic values it at JP¥4,270. Note the wide gap in analyst price targets? This implies to us that there is a fairly broad range of possible scenarios for the underlying business.
Taking a look at the bigger picture now, one of the ways we can understand these forecasts is to see how they compare to both past performance and industry growth estimates.

sum: SoftBank Group shares have been on a tear, climbing 13% on Wednesday as investors shook off the company's quarterly losses and piled back into Japanese technology names. The advance follows a broader rally across Asian tech stocks, with traders pointing to renewed buying in chipmakers and a pullback in oil prices that eased inflation worries. The upbeat market backdrop had already taken shape before SoftBank's results hit the tape, and the stock's resilience suggests shareholders are treating the loss as a one-off rather than a verdict on the group's AI strategy.

That loss is considerable. For the three months through September 30, 2026 — the second quarter of SoftBank's fiscal year — the group posted a net loss attributable to owners of ¥1.12 trillion, a sharp reversal from a ¥2.50 trillion profit in the same period a year earlier, according to Reuters.

A ¥597.25 billion loss tied to revised procurement plans for power generation equipment for U.S. AI data centers accounted for a large chunk of the damage, with higher financing costs adding further pressure. The write-down stems from changed specifications for the power supply infrastructure underpinning SoftBank's American AI projects — a reminder that the group's aggressive buildout carries real balance-sheet risk.

On the expansion front, SoftBank has signed joint development agreements with Grab Holdings and Petroleum Sarawak Berhad (PETROS) to build AI infrastructure in Malaysia. The partners have announced an initial joint capital commitment of US$1.85 billion, with SoftBank slated to contribute US$1 billion, Grab US$750 million and PETROS US$100 million. Longer term, the trio is targeting at least five gigawatts of AI computing capacity. The capital contributions are proposed rather than funds already paid in.

Less welcome is the news from China, where the authority for the security review of foreign investment has blocked SoftBank's acquisition of ABB's Chinese robotics business. SoftBank said Friday it remains in close dialogue with ABB and that both sides are working constructively on the transaction, though no final outcome for the broader takeover has been disclosed.

SoftBank's Robotics Deal Hinges on Whether a Smaller ABB Package Can Still Make Sense
sum: SoftBank's push into industrial robotics now comes down to a question of scope rather than ambition. With Beijing blocking its purchase of ABB's robotics unit outright, the Japanese conglomerate and the Swiss engineering group are weighing whether carving out the Chinese operations — or handing the business to a different buyer altogether — can rescue a transaction that was meant to anchor Masayoshi Son's "Physical AI" strategy.

The regulatory obstacle is already explicit. SoftBank disclosed on Friday that China's authority for security reviews of foreign investment has prohibited the acquisition of ABB's robotics business within the country. Both sides, the company said, remain in close contact and are working constructively on the deal. Reuters reported a day earlier that removing the Chinese robotics operations from the transaction was under consideration, a possible route around the blockade provided the two sides can agree on viable terms.

Bloomberg added a further twist: ABB is simultaneously exploring a sale to another interested party, with valuations of USD 2–3 billion cited in reports. A spin-off is also on the table. Under the carve-out scenario, the Chinese business would be placed in a separate company with other owners, leaving SoftBank to take the remainder.

Talks are at an early stage and could still collapse. The original agreement, signed on October 8, 2025, valued the entire robotics division at USD 5.375 billion — the figure Reuters put at USD 5.4 billion. Neither company has yet named new terms or a revised closing date.
SoftBank shares rose 3.9% on Friday. For investors, the more consequential issue is what the group might ultimately acquire, and at what price.

ABB Robotics generated USD 2.3 billion in revenue in 2024 and employed roughly 7,000 people. Those figures describe the division as a whole; any residual business would have to be judged on its own earning power and setup. A geographically altered acquisition therefore amounts to more than a organizational tweak — it changes the size of what SoftBank would own, and the economics turn on the activities that remain and the price agreed for them.

sum: SoftBank Group shares rose 4.4% on Tuesday even as anxiety over the profitability of artificial intelligence rippled through global financial markets. That divergence captures the central tension now surrounding the Japanese conglomerate: investors remain drawn to its sprawling AI exposure, yet they are increasingly demanding evidence that the spending will eventually pay off.

The scale of SoftBank's commitments explains why it has become a bellwether for AI investment. Reuters reports a $64.6 billion stake in OpenAI alongside a 90% holding in Arm. Those positions offer a stake in a technological transformation, but their value hinges on whether the underlying expectations hold up — a condition that carries particular weight given the sheer size of the bets.

Skepticism is already visible in the company's credit protection. The spread on SoftBank's credit default swaps has climbed to a four-year high, a signal that unease extends beyond equity holders. Worries about heavier borrowing and delayed returns are cited by Reuters as pressure points, making the timing of the group's investments as important as their scale.

That link between funding needs and payoff timelines is what makes SoftBank both compelling and demanding. Weighing the promise of its AI portfolio against rising return requirements is now the central task for anyone assessing the stock. Size alone, in this environment, no longer convinces.

Nowhere is the gap between ambition and execution more visible than at SB Energy. The unit filed for an IPO in September at a potential valuation of $50 billion — yet it currently operates no data centers at all. Media reports indicate the listing has been pushed back to December or later.

That combination sits at the heart of the SoftBank risk. The contracted business offers a credible outlook provided the necessary infrastructure arrives on schedule. Until operations begin, however, the valuation leans heavily on the company's ability to align construction, financing and customer uptake. SB Energy is also heavily dependent on OpenAI, pairing an uncertain capital-markets timetable with pronounced customer concentration — a combination that argues against generous valuations of expected revenue while operational delivery remains pending.

sum: The Nikkei 225 began trading higher on the Tokyo Stock Exchange on November 5, opening at 62,384.73 yen, up 196.10 yen (0.32%) from the previous trading day. Buying led the market, carrying over the momentum from gains in all three major U.S. stock indexes the prior day.

Two factors pushed the market up. One was the firm performance of the U.S. stock market as it digested the results of the U.S. midterm elections. The other was a sharp drop in crude oil prices as views spread that tensions in the Middle East were easing. Lower energy costs support investor sentiment through both corporate earnings and household burdens.
Among blue-chip shares, Toyota Motor (7203.T) surged, while Sony Group (6758.T) and index-heavyweight Fast Retailing (9983.T) were quoted higher.

On the other hand, artificial intelligence (AI) and semiconductor-related shares saw notable declines. SoftBank Group (9984.T), Tokyo Electron (8035.T), and Advantest (6857.T) all fell sharply, as caution over the direction of AI regulation continued to simmer.

In the previous day's trading on November 4, these three semiconductor and AI-related stocks alone pushed the Nikkei 225 down by about 1,241 yen at one point. Selling tends to concentrate in stocks with large index weightings, and this structure continues to amplify swings across the broader market.

Among market participants, the near-term focus is whether buybacks will emerge in the sharply fallen semiconductor shares. On the previous day, some stocks such as Fast Retailing and Nintendo (7974.T) rose, so the market was not uniformly lower. Some see the fact that buying interest is not one-sided as a sign of the market's underlying resilience.

On the overseas front, reports on vote counting in the U.S. midterm elections were also coming in during Tokyo trading hours, and market participants are focused on how U.S. long-term interest rates and foreign exchange rates react. Domestically, earnings announcements from companies such as IHI (7013.T), Mitsubishi Corp (8058.T), and NTT (9432.T) are scheduled during trading hours, and stock price reactions to individual earnings results could divide winners and losers within sectors.

sum: Artificial intelligence giant OpenAI, after shelving its IPO plans, is reportedly in talks with investors for a new funding round, targeting at least $30 billion at a valuation of approximately $1.4 trillion. The news drove a sharp rebound in major backer SoftBank Group (9984.T) shares on the Tokyo stock market.

According to Bloomberg, citing people familiar with the matter, the valuation basis for this round excludes the newly raised capital, and discussions remain in early stages with terms subject to change. The report noted that given OpenAI's strong revenue growth, the financing demand is primarily investor-driven.

Sources revealed that the round is intended to serve as "bridge financing," providing the company with needed capital before a formal initial public offering, replacing the capital injection an IPO would have provided. If the financing is completed at a $1.4 trillion valuation, OpenAI would once again surpass the valuation level achieved by longtime rival Anthropic in its most recent funding round.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman recently made clear that the company will not go public in 2026. He said Tuesday that amid increasingly severe AI safety concerns, the company wants to avoid the pressures faced by newly listed companies.

Altman told Fortune: "I think by the end of this decade, taking on roughly a 10% chance of killing everyone is unacceptable." The remarks were in response to warnings from safety researchers that AI could pose existential risks to humanity.

He noted that the company is currently adjusting to a "new level" of AI capability and the additional safety requirements that come with it, and believes investors will remain patient with its IPO plans.

OpenAI completed a $122 billion funding round in March this year at a valuation of $852 billion. That round was originally positioned as the final private placement before an IPO, with the market widely expecting the company to list within the year.

The stock slid 3.1% to 6,154.0 yen after Bloomberg reported that Oracle had sent a force-majeure notice to a Blue Owl unit developing Project Jupiter.

Oracle issued the notice over potential delays in securing power for Project Jupiter, a large data-center campus that is part of Stargate, the $500 billion AI infrastructure initiative involving Oracle, OpenAI and SoftBank Group.

Oracle is seeking to protect itself from payment obligations if the project is delayed and fails to come online in 2028 as planned, according to people familiar with the matter cited by Reuters and Bloomberg.

The development has raised broader questions over whether the huge amounts of capital being committed to AI infrastructure can be deployed on schedule, particularly as developers face constraints around power, construction and financing, according to Reuters.

The timing is particularly sensitive for SoftBank Group, which has been increasing its leverage to finance its AI strategy. The company raised $11.1 billion through dollar- and euro-denominated bonds this week, with the proceeds aimed in part at funding its investment in OpenAI.

The Oracle development comes as credit investors become more selective toward AI-related debt. Reuters reported that spreads on AI-linked bonds had widened to about 115 basis points, versus 78 basis points for the broader market, while hyperscaler debt issuance is expected to rise sharply as companies finance data centers and chips.

SoftBank's Record Retail Bond Masks the Real Story: A $60 Billion OpenAI Pledge and a Widening Fundi
sum: The Japanese conglomerate's latest debt sale is historic in scale, but it reveals just how far the company's ambitions now outrun its balance sheet.

SoftBank Group is preparing to sell roughly $6.3 billion in seven-year bonds to Japanese retail investors, a transaction that would mark the largest corporate bond offering to individuals in Japan's history. The notes, carrying a coupon between 4.3 and 4.9 percent, are slated to be priced on September 4, with the subscription window running from September 7 through September 16.

This marks the third retail bond issuance of the year for the Masayoshi Son-led holding company, following earlier deals worth 418 billion and 260 billion yen. The sheer frequency of these offerings underscores a growing reliance on domestic retail investors as a lender of last resort — banks have shown little appetite for underwriting the full risk of SoftBank's AI ambitions.

The funding gap tells the more striking story. Even after this latest round, SoftBank faces a shortfall of more than $20 billion, leading market observers to expect an offshore bond sale as the likely next step. The scale of the company's commitments is staggering: SoftBank has pledged more than $60 billion to OpenAI and has separately sought a $10 billion margin loan secured against its OpenAI stake. Reports indicate the company is participating with roughly $30 billion in OpenAI's current funding round, which values the ChatGPT developer at approximately $852 billion.

The bond sale arrives as SoftBank's stock struggles to reflect the underlying momentum in its portfolio. The shares traded at €27.04 after a 4.9 percent decline, extending a weekly loss of 13 percent. The secondary article notes a slightly different trading snapshot — a 4.4 percent drop to €27.16 — but both point to the same trend: investors are punishing the stock despite a billion-dollar gain from its Intel stake and an uptick in the Vision Fund's valuation, driven by ByteDance and OpenAI-linked holdings. The RSI reading of 38 suggests the stock is approaching oversold territory.
Beyond the OpenAI bet, SoftBank is pushing into the physical infrastructure that powers artificial intelligence.

The filing, submitted to the Securities and Exchange Commission, places Intel far ahead of SoftBank's next-largest U.S. holdings. Symbotic stock came in second at around $1.79 billion, or roughly 10% of the total, while T-Mobile U.S. stock added another $1.68 billion, or about 9%, according to Yahoo Finance. The remainder of the portfolio — a collection of fintech names including Klarna, Chime, eToro, Nu Holdings, and Inter & Co — amounted to a marginal slice of the whole.

The Intel position reflects a substantial escalation of SoftBank's existing exposure to the chipmaker. SoftBank Group chair Masayoshi Son's firm had previously committed a $2 billion strategic investment into Intel that closed in the third quarter of 2025, according to Yahoo Finance.

Intel's second-quarter fiscal 2026 results showed revenue of $16.128 billion, a 25.4% increase from the prior-year period, with the Data Center and AI segment posting a 59% gain to reach $6.262 billion. For the third quarter of 2026, Intel set a revenue outlook of $15.8 billion to $16.8 billion.

SoftBank's Intel bet figures into a broader picture of gains and losses at the Japanese conglomerate. The firm reported first-quarter net income of 347.3 billion yen, or approximately $2.2 billion, driven by a 1.3 trillion yen gain on Intel stock. Intel stock has risen close to 400% on a year-over-year basis. SoftBank's cumulative investment in OpenAI is expected to reach approximately $64.6 billion upon completion of a third planned tranche in October 2026, representing an ownership stake of roughly 13%, the company said.

The 13F filing covers positions held as of June 30. Institutional money managers with more than $100 million in U.S. equities must submit the form no later than 45 days after each quarter's close. Even measured against SoftBank's well-documented history of outsized single-asset wagers, the Intel stake is notable: in raw dollar terms, it exceeds the combined value of every other U.S. equity position the firm disclosed.

sum: Растет неопределенность в отношении перспектив «Проекта Звездных врат», масштабной инициативы капиталовложений в инфраструктуру искусственного интеллекта (ИИ). Акции SoftBank Group (SBG, 9984.T), возглавляющей проект, упали до минимума за три с половиной месяца на Токийской фондовой бирже 30 июля, упав ровно до половины исторического максимума, зафиксированного в июне. Между тем, долгосрочный восходящий тренд американского полупроводникового гиганта Nvidia (NVDA), ключевого технологического партнера в проекте, также повернул вниз. Одновременный разворот двух акций, которые привели к ралли ИИ в Японии и США, быстро усиливает тревогу инвесторов.

Акции SBG были проданы на 5% за день до 4500 иен, что составляет ровно половину рекордного максимума в 9074 иен, установленного 2 июня. Непосредственным толчком к этому падению стал прогноз прибыли британской дочерней компании Arm Holdings, занимающейся разработкой микросхем, который не оправдал ожиданий рынка. Прогноз выручки Arm на квартал с июля по сентябрь 2026 года, опубликованный 29 июля, прогнозировал существенный рост в годовом исчислении, но опасения по поводу ухудшения цен на рынке смартфонов — особенно резкого роста цен на память — спровоцировали резкую распродажу акций Arm. Затем этот спад коснулся материнской компании SBG.
Прогноз Arm на квартал с июля по сентябрь 2026 года (второй квартал) был следующим: как выручка, так и прибыль на акцию превысили консенсус-оценки.

Arm также понизила прогноз роста доходов от роялти за весь год с «около 20%» до «высоких процентов». Компания сослалась на сокращение производства производителями смартфонов из-за роста цен на память — специфического проявления ухудшения ценовой конъюнктуры на рынке смартфонов, упомянутого ранее. Несмотря на то, что выручка и прибыль на акцию превысили консенсус, этот сигнал замедления был встречен с пренебрежением, и акции Arm упали на 8% в ходе торгов после закрытия.

В связи с этим Deutsche Bank понизил рейтинг акций SBG с «Покупать» до «Держать». Банк отметил снижение привлекательности оценки после недавнего резкого ралли и влияние обесценивания иены на оценку активов SBG, включая ее долю в Arm.

sum: During the Asian trading session on July 28, the Nikkei 225 Index dropped over 4%, driven by a sharp sell-off in the semiconductor sector. Key stocks like Kioxia, Advantest, and Tokyo Electron faced significant declines. Market sentiment was dampened by investor concerns over Nvidia’s circular financing model and its associated credit risks. Furthermore, reports regarding China’s progress in domestic DUV lithography production have fueled anxieties over future competitiveness for Japanese suppliers. This downturn reflects a broader cooling of investor confidence in the AI infrastructure chain, spreading from U.S. markets to Japan’s high-tech sector.

TradingKey - During the Asian trading session on July 28, Japanese stocks opened lower and accelerated their slide. As of press time, the Nikkei 225 Index fell over 4%, briefly dropping below 62,000 points to hit its lowest level since late May, while the Topix Index fell nearly 3%. The semiconductor sector collapsed almost across the board, becoming the primary drag on the broader market.

Among individual stocks, as of press time, memory chip giant Kioxia Holdings plunged over 18% intraday, marking its largest single-day drop since November last year and leading the Nikkei index lower. Advantest and Tokyo Electron both tumbled over 10%, while SoftBank Group also weakened, dropping more than 6%.

The selling pressure was primarily driven by a combination of multiple negative factors. On the news front, Nvidia ( NVDA) is in talks for AI infrastructure projects totaling over $750 billion and plans to provide approximately $250 billion in financing guarantees for OpenAI. Meanwhile, there are reports that Chinese state-owned enterprises have initiated the production of domestically developed immersion DUV lithography machines, with plans to deliver about 5 units this year, and SMIC, Hua Hong Semiconductor, and ChangXin Memory Technologies are on the list of first-batch customers.

sum: The global sell-off in AI chip stocks intensified on Friday as panic swept from Wall Street across Asian markets. Japanese equities became the epicenter of the rout after the opening bell, with SoftBank Group shares plunging more than 9% at one point and memory chip giant Kioxia cratering over 15% on patent litigation headwinds, dragging the Nikkei sharply lower.

The trigger for this tech rout stems from unprecedented skepticism over the sustainability of massive capital expenditure on artificial intelligence. Even though contract chipmaking leader TSMC just announced it was raising its full-year capex budget to between $60 billion and $64 billion (approximately NT$1.9 trillion to NT$2.1 trillion), investors refused to cheer the news, instead pivoting their focus to the potential risks of industry overinvestment.

In the Japanese market, SoftBank Group (9984.T-JP) tumbled more than 9%, chip equipment maker Tokyo Electron (8035.T-JP) plunged over 8%, and test equipment giant Advantest (6857.T-JP) sank more than 10%. Japanese memory chip maker Kioxia (285A.T-JP) suffered an even steeper decline of over 15%, hit by a double whammy: broad market weakness and a ruling by a U.S. federal jury in Texas that the company infringed a Viasat computer storage technology patent and must pay $229 million (approximately NT$7.5 billion) in damages. South Korea's stock market was closed for a public holiday, temporarily escaping the carnage, but its bellwether SK Hynix (SKHY.US) had already seen its U.S.-traded ADR plummet over 13% the previous day, setting the stage for Friday's Asian sell-off.

The sell-off was a direct extension of the semiconductor sector's collapse in U.S. markets. Overnight on Wall Street, the Nasdaq Composite tumbled 1.47%, with chip stocks once again serving as the epicenter of the carnage. The VanEck Semiconductor ETF fell nearly 4%, Arm (ARM.US) dropped more than 5%, and heavyweight names including Micron Technology (MU.US), AMD (AMD.US), and Broadcom (AVGO.US) all declined more than 5%.

Addressing the extreme market panic, Ortus Advisors strategist Andrew Jackson argued that the sell-off reflects concentrated unwinding of crowded AI trades rather than deterioration in the sector's long-term fundamentals.

sum: Masayoshi Son, left, chairman and CEO of SoftBank Group, speaks as Mark Chen, chief research officer for OpenAI, listens during a talk at their business event at a hotel in Tokyo on June 16. (AP file photo)

Worries about a bubble in artificial intelligence investments are absurd, SoftBank Group’s CEO Masayoshi Son said Tuesday, deriding such doubts as backward and akin to questioning the use of cars and planes.
“To ask whether AI is a bubble is a foolish question,” Son told executives at an annual company event in Tokyo. “AI will transform our lives completely, and do so in a way that generates profits.”
“Those who refuse to evolve are closing down their world. Those who condemn AI are themselves spitting upward,” Son added.

Financial markets have recently been swept by waves of concern that the meteoric rise in share prices of companies like Nvidia, and massive investments in data centers, might not yield returns that match hopes for huge profits from AI.
Son founded SoftBank more than four decades ago and is a pioneer in Japan’s technology investments. He was an early supporter of AI and has invested tens of billions of dollars in related companies.

Son said he estimates that almost $5 trillion in investments will be needed annually and globally to expand data centers, increase production of computer chips and provide energy systems and other infrastructure for AI.

He envisions a society dominated by 100 trillion AI agents, supported by a transition from natural gas to nuclear fusion for power. Despite this bullish outlook, SoftBank faces significant volatility as delays in OpenAI’s IPO extend monetization timelines and weigh on stock performance. While the company aggressively expands its AI footprint, market skepticism regarding valuations and high-growth delivery remains a primary risk factor impacting investor confidence and share price stability.

TradingKey - During Asian trading hours on July 14, SoftBank Group CEO Masayoshi Son predicted at the company's annual corporate meeting in Tokyo that by 2040, the AI sector would require an annual investment of $5 trillion (approximately 800 trillion yen). He flatly dismissed market concerns about an AI bubble, calling the question itself "absurd."

Son is known for his bold bets on transformative technologies. 'Five trillion dollars a year, you might think that is unbelievable, but I firmly believe this is the cost required,' he said at the meeting. He further argued the feasibility of his business model: 'By 2040, if AI revenue accounts for 20% of global GDP, then an annual expenditure of 800 trillion yen is just a rounding error.' However, he did not elaborate on the specific calculation basis for the $5 trillion forecast.

Son explicitly refuted market doubts regarding an AI valuation bubble. He believes that those who ask such questions 'don't understand what AI is at all.' This aligns with his consistent previous position that 'calling AI a bubble is a blasphemy against AI.' In his view, the revolutionary impact of AI is still in the early stages of being unleashed.

Regarding the energy support required for computing power, Son also made an assessment. He expects that by 2040, the electricity demand of AI data centers will reach 3 terawatts, equivalent to 1.8 times the current global power consumption. On the supply side, it will initially rely mainly on natural gas power generation, but with technological evolution, nuclear fusion is expected to replace natural gas as the primary energy source in about 15 years.

sum: A record 976 executives at publicly listed companies in Japan received total compensation of ¥100 million or more in the fiscal year ended March 2026, an increase of 88 individuals from the previous year. The number of companies with such highly paid executives also reached 407, breaking through the 400-company mark for the first time. Fueled by the artificial intelligence boom, earnings have surged—particularly at semiconductor-related firms—and the widespread adoption of performance-linked compensation systems, including stock-based pay, is clearly driving up executive remuneration.

Tokyo Shoko Research, a private credit research firm, compiled data from annual securities reports filed by listed companies by the end of June. The number of executives earning ¥100 million or more reached its highest level since disclosure became mandatory in the fiscal year ended March 2010. The number of executives earning ¥1 billion (approximately $6.2 million) or more also rose sharply to 20, up from 15 the previous year.

Topping the compensation rankings was Rene Haas, a director at SoftBank Group (9984.T), whose total pay amounted to ¥6.139 billion. Haas also serves as CEO of Arm Holdings, the British semiconductor design giant under SoftBank Group's umbrella, and the bulk of his compensation is believed to have come from stock-based awards granted by Arm.

Ranking second was Stacy Smith, chairman of Kioxia Holdings, with ¥4.431 billion. The company has come to dominate the market for advanced memory chips used in AI applications, and its market capitalization has soared to the top spot in Japan amid expanding AI-related investment. Smith's compensation surged roughly 15-fold compared to the previous year.
In third place was Hiroki Totoki, president and CEO of Sony Group (6758.T), with ¥2.757 billion. Totoki's pay roughly doubled from the prior year following his appointment as CEO in April 2025.

The survey results vividly illustrate a structural shift in executive compensation at major Japanese corporations. The traditional system centered on fixed salaries is giving way to a framework where stock-based and performance-linked compensation—tied to share prices and earnings—account for a larger proportion.

SoftBank reportedly reopens talks for $10bn loan backed by OpenAI stake
sum: Investing.com -- SoftBank Group has reportedly resumed discussions with a group of lenders for a $10 billion loan secured by its ownership stake in OpenAI. The Japanese technology investor had previously attempted to arrange similar financing but faced resistance from banks concerned about the challenges of valuing private companies.

SoftBank is now offering to guarantee repayment of the loan to address lender concerns. This structure would give banks recourse to SoftBank if the OpenAI shares used as collateral decline in value, according to a report from Reuters News.

SoftBank has emerged as one of OpenAI's largest investors under founder Masayoshi Son's strategy to position the conglomerate as a leading force in artificial intelligence investment. SoftBank has committed over $60 billion to OpenAI and related AI infrastructure projects, including the Stargate data center venture announced with OpenAI and Oracle.

The financing takes the form of a margin loan, which operates as a line of credit. The lending consortium is expected to include Goldman Sachs Group Inc (NYSE:GS), JPMorgan Chase & Co (NYSE:JPM), and Mizuho Financial Group, the report said.

SoftBank has used debt and asset-backed financing extensively to fund its investments. The company explored a $5 billion margin loan backed by shares in chip designer Arm Holdings, whose stock price has risen amid investor interest in AI.

Banks initially rejected SoftBank's request for the loan to be backed only by its OpenAI stake. Under that structure, lenders would have no claim on SoftBank beyond the shares if the collateral lost value, and SoftBank would not have been required to repay the debt, the report said.

The negotiations reflect increased caution among lenders toward loans secured by stakes in private companies, whose valuations are more difficult to determine and whose shares are less liquid than publicly traded stock.

A listed OpenAI would serve as a benchmark for one of its largest positions, potentially narrowing the conglomerate discount that has long weighed on the stock, Takei said. "News of an IPO delay naturally dampens those expectations," he said.

Goldman Sachs Group and Morgan Stanley are advising OpenAI on a possible public offering that could come as early as this fall, noting that the company has already filed confidential listing documents with U.S. securities regulators.

SoftBank's exposure to OpenAI sits at the center of a complex financial picture the company has been navigating for months. An effort by SoftBank to raise at least $6 billion through a margin loan collateralized by its OpenAI holdings stalled earlier this month, with lenders citing difficulty pricing a stake in a private company with no public market valuation. Masayoshi Son Is Betting It All on American AI
sum: The 39th floor penthouse of SoftBank’s downtown Tokyo headquarters is not your usual featureless C-suite. Bedecked floor to ceiling in sallow pine, it was created to evoke the calming ambience of a traditional Japanese village, with exposed timber couplings and the refrain of gurgling water. “I designed it personally,” SoftBank founder Masayoshi Son tells TIME in an exclusive interview, gazing at the sweeping vista dominated by Edo-period imperial gardens.

They may be digs that hark back to a bygone era, but from his lofty perch Son is very much focused on the horizon. And the next one. After making a fortune in software and parlaying that into telecoms and a raft of tech ventures, Son is now pivoting SoftBank’s $180 billion war chest into artificial intelligence (AI) with unbridled zeal. Deals include taking control of chip firms Arm, Graphcore, and Ampere Computing, as well as self-driving car start-up Wayve, $2 billion into Intel, plus some $40 billion into ChatGPT creator OpenAI—with reports of an additional $30 billion for the latter in the pipeline.

“ChatGPT can give me quicker, more precise, more detailed answers,” Son, 68, gushes. “I can debate, bounce ideas, brainstorm, it’s amazing. But this is the beginning. It’s going to be a billion times more [smart]. Super intelligence is coming soon.”

Artificial super intelligence, or ASI, will become “10,000 times smarter” than humans within a decade, Son predicts, grandiosely telling a shareholders' meeting that he was “born to realize” the breakthrough. ASI combined with physical AI such as humanoid robotics will comprise 10% of global GDP in 10 to 15 years, he tells TIME, rising to 30% over 30 years. “AI models are evolving very quickly,” he says. “So this is going to be a massive industry.”

Exciting stuff. Though Son’s high-risk, even higher-leveraged investment style has courted disaster almost as much as success. His $20 million investment in Chinese e-commerce giant Alibaba was worth close to $200 billion at its peak and arguably history’s greatest investment. But the $18.5 billion he plowed into the now bankrupt office-sharing venture WeWork lists among history’s most foolhardy, spurring Son to sequester himself from public view for 18 months.

sum: There have been many AI-driven selloffs in the three years since ChatGPT burst into the mainstream. Nothing, though, quite rivals the rout rippling through stock and credit markets this week.

For one, there’s the sheer speed and breadth of it. In the span of two days, hundreds of billions of dollars were wiped off the value of stocks, bonds and loans of companies big and small across Silicon Valley. Software stocks were at the epicenter, plunging so much that the value of those tracked in an iShares ETF has now dropped almost $1 trillion over the past seven days.

For another, this drubbing, unlike many previous ones, was triggered not by fears of a bubble but rather concern that AI is on the verge of supplanting the business models of a wide swathe of companies that doomsayers have long predicted were at risk.

“I don’t think it is an overreaction,” said Michael O’Rourke, chief market strategist at Jonestrading. “For two years, we have been talking about how AI is going to change the world and that it is a multi-generational technology. In the past few weeks, we have seen signs of it in practice.”

The spark was innocuous on its face: AI startup Anthropic PBC released a new tool for legal work, like reviewing contracts. On its own, the product isn’t seen as a game-changer — yet. But coming after a year in which Anthropic’s coding tools helped transform software development — part of a broader wave of AI innovation — the four-paragraph launch announcement was taken extremely seriously.
“While today it’s legal tech, tomorrow it might be sales or marketing or finance,” wrote Jackson Ader, an analyst at KeyBanc.

Adding to investor unease, even companies long seen as the prime beneficiaries of the AI boom are showing signs of fatigue. In earnings reports, Alphabet Inc. said capital spending on AI would be higher than anticipated, while Arm Holdings Plc issued a revenue forecast that missed expectations. Both stocks fell in after-hours trading.

It was actually a relatively light news month for Arm, but a skeptical investing public tended to take profits in December after a strong run to the year for semiconductors.

On December 15, sell-side analyst Jim Schneider of Goldman Sachs downgraded Arm shares to the ignominious "Sell" rating, from his prior "Neutral" rating. "Sell" ratings are fairly rare among Wall Street analysts, with "Neutral" usually indicating skepticism and "Sell" indicating outright pessimism.

Schneider flagged Arm along with a handful of other semiconductor stocks that had been disappointments in the early stages of the AI buildout, claiming Arm had "limited ability" to leverage the AI cycle. He also pointed out risks to Arm's "business model transition" as it moves from licensing IP blocks to full sub-systems, and even explores making its own chips, potentially putting it competition with its customers.

In truth, the downgrade doesn't seem that reasonable, since Arm licenses its architecture to Nvidia (NVDA -5.47%) for its Grace CPUs, as well as most of the cloud giants for their in-house server CPU designs. Last quarter's revenue grew 34%, so it doesn't appear that growth is a big problem right now.

This decline comes as the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite fell 1.81% overnight, dragged by losses in Oracle, Broadcom, Nvidia and other AI plays.

The losses in Oracle came after the Financial Times reported on Wednesday that Blue Owl Capital's plans to finance the cloud infrastructure company's $10 billion Michigan data center had stalled. Tech-focused SoftBank has seen sharp volatility in its stock over the past month as fears over AI-related spending have gripped the market.

At the start of the year, the group had revealed plans to invest $500 billion in AI infrastructure in the U.S. along with OpenAI, Oracle and other partners, and in September it announced five new U.S. AI data center sites under Stargate, OpenAI's overarching AI infrastructure platform.

items.t: SoftBank CEO Masayoshi Son Just Delivered Incredible News to Nvidia Investors
sum: Masayoshi Son is a legendary investor from Japan, best known for founding the technology-focused holding company SoftBank Group. With hundreds of billions in assets under management, SoftBank hasn't been shy about getting involved in the artificial intelligence (AI) revolution.

Perhaps unsurprisingly, the investment firm took a sizable position in Nvidia (NVDA -5.47%) over the last several years, and benefited handsomely from the chip designer's influence in the AI landscape.

However, last month, investors learned that SoftBank had sold its entire stake in Nvidia -- netting nearly $6 billion in proceeds. While this move initially led some to question whether SoftBank had lost confidence in Nvidia, Son recently put those fears to rest.

Earlier this month, an organization called the Future Investment Initiative held a summit in Tokyo that featured a number of business leaders and entrepreneurs. During one of the presentations, Son was asked about the rationale behind SoftBank's sale of Nvidia stock.

He got straight to the point, replying that he respects Nvidia's visionary CEO, Jensen Huang. He followed up by saying he hadn't wanted to sell a "single share" and joked that he was "crying" over the investment decision.

To me, it sounds like Son still thinks quite highly of the chipmaker. While this should ease shareholders' concerns, we still need to uncover exactly why SoftBank ultimately decided to make this tough decision.

Shortly after the inauguration of President Donald Trump back in January, a small team of business leaders assembled at the White House to announce Project Stargate. In essence, it's a joint venture between Oracle, SoftBank, and OpenAI that is expected to invest $500 billion into building AI infrastructure in the U.S. over the next four years.

SoftBank Corp. and Yaskawa Electric Corporation Begin Collaboration on Social Implementation of "Physical AI" Utilizing AI-RAN
sum: SoftBank Corp. (President & CEO: Junichi Miyakawa, "SoftBank") and Yaskawa Electric Corporation (Representative Director, President: Masahiro Ogawa, "Yaskawa Electric") have agreed to collaborate on the social implementation of "Physical AI*1", leveraging SoftBank's AI-RAN initiative and Yaskawa Electric's AI robotics and signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) to formalize the collaboration.

As the first phase of their partnership, SoftBank and Yaskawa Electric have jointly developed a use case for an office-oriented Physical AI robot that integrates with building management systems and utilizes AI running on MEC (Multi-access Edge Computing). Conventional robots have been designed to perform specific tasks and have not been capable of handling multiple tasks simultaneously. However, by leveraging AI operating on MEC, it is possible to integrate and analyze various types of information in real time, accurately assess situations, and provide optimal instructions to robots. As a result, robots can now flexibly perform a wider variety of tasks, realizing "multi-skilled functionality" by enabling a single unit to take on multiple roles.
A demonstration of this robot is scheduled to take place at the 2025 International Robot Exhibition (iREX 2025), which will be held at Tokyo Big Sight from December 3 to 6, 2025.

- *1Physical AI refers to technology that enables robots to analyze and interpret data from sensors, cameras, and external systems through AI, allowing them to perform flexible and complex physical movements based on AI-driven decisions.

As Japan faces challenges such as labor shortages resulting from a declining birthrate and an aging population, as well as increasing complexity in business operations, the need for automation and labor-saving solutions is growing across many industries. The use of AI and robotics is becoming increasingly important to meet these needs. However, in environments where large numbers of people move around, such as office buildings, hospitals, schools, and department stores, it has been difficult to promote automation. These conditions often require complex decision-making and flexible responses to unpredictable situations.

sum: SoftBank Group will raise about ¥500 billion ($3.2 billion) from retail investors at a coupon of 3.98% — the highest on a yen-denominated senior bond from the company in more than 15 years.

The rate on the unsecured seven-year note was set near the upper end of the previously announced range of between 3.5% and 4.1%, according to a term sheet from the company today. The last time it sold a like bond with a coupon that high was in 2009 at 4.52%.

Mom-and-pop investors have been increasingly drawn to the corporate bond market in search of higher returns, after the Bank of Japan ended its negative interest policy in March 2024. Yields on Japanese government bonds, which serve as benchmark for corporate issues, have climbed amid rising inflation and market caution over Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s fiscal spending package.

“With interest rates rising, individual investors are also finding corporate bonds more attractive,” said Kazuma Ogino, senior credit analyst at Nomura Securities. Corporate bond issuance has reached record levels, making it harder for companies to sell bonds to institutional investors, he said, pointing out that SoftBank is one of Japan’s largest bond issuers.

While higher yields have raised companies’ borrowing costs, their appetite for funding remains strong. Japanese firms have raised a record ¥2.79 trillion through yen-denominated retail bonds so far in 2025, surpassing the previous high last year, according to compiled data.
The proceeds from the bond sale will partly be used to repay a bridge loan in connection with an additional investment in U.S.-based OpenAI.

Earlier this month, SoftBank Group announced second quarter net income that beat analyst expectations, on gains from its investments in artificial intelligence, according to its financial disclosure statements. One of the biggest contributors to this growth was its Vision Fund, which benefited from rising valuations of unlisted AI-related holdings such as OpenAI.

Although the Nvidia sale surprised some investors, it isn't the first time SoftBank has exited the U.S. chip giant. Its Vision Fund had accumulated roughly $4 billion worth of Nvidia shares in 2017 before selling out entirely in early 2019.

"We want to provide a lot of investment opportunities for investors, while we can still maintain financial strength," said SoftBank's chief financial officer, Yoshimitsu Goto, during an investor presentation.
While the decision to unload Nvidia shares may have caught some investors off guard, it isn't SoftBank's first exit from the U.S. chip heavyweight.

The company's Vision Fund was an early Nvidia supporter, reportedly building a $4 billion stake in 2017 before fully divesting in January 2019. Despite the latest sale, SoftBank remains closely tied to Nvidia through its broader business interests.
"This is a bullish signal on the theme from SoftBank doubling down and not a bearish sign in our view," said Dan Ives, global head of technology research at Wedbush Securities.

While OpenAI is central to SoftBank's GenAI portfolio, hardware remains a priority as well, mostly through its stake in British chip designer Arm, with which SoftBank is co-developing products, said Rolf Bulk, equity research analyst at New Street Research.
